etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English quiver, from Anglo-Norman quivre, from Old Dutch cocare (source of Dutch koker, and cognate to Old English cocer (“quiver, case”)), from Proto-West Germanic *kokar (“container”), said to be from Hunnic, possibly from Proto-Mongolic *kökexür (“leather vessel for liquids”); see there for more. Replaced early modern cocker, the inherited reflex of that West Germanic word.

definitions.definition: (weaponry) A container for arrows, crossbow bolts or darts, such as those fired from a bow, crossbow or blowgun.

quote.citation: 1598–1599 (first performance), William Shakespeare, “Much Adoe about Nothing”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i], line 271:
quote.text: Don Pedro: Nay, if Cupid have not spent all his quiver in Venice, thou wilt quake for this shortly.

quote.citation: 1786, Francis Grose, A Treatise on Ancient Armour and Weapons, page 39:
quote.text: Arrows were carried in quiver, called also an arrow case, which served for the magazine, arrows for immediate use were worn in the girdle.

definitions.definition: (figuratively) A ready storage location for figurative tools or weapons.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English quiver, cwiver, from Old English *cwifer, probably related to cwic (“alive”).

quote.citation: c. 1596–1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Second Part of Henry the Fourth, […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii], line 281:
quote.text: [...] there was a little quiver fellow, and 'a would manage you his piece thus; and 'a would about and about, and come you in and come you in.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English quiveren, probably from the adjective.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To shake or move with slight and tremulous motion.

quote.citation: c. 1588–1593 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Lamentable Tragedy of Titus Andronicus”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene iii], line 12:
quote.text: The birds chaunt melodie on euerie buſh,  The ſnakes[sic – meaning ſnake] lies rolled in the chearefull ſunne,  The greene leaues quiuer with the cooling winde,  And make a checkerd ſhadow on the ground: [...]

quote.citation: 1712 (date written), [Joseph] Addison, Cato, a Tragedy. […], London:  […]  J[acob] Tonson, […], published 1713, →OCLC, Act I, scene iv, page 2:
quote.text: And left the limbs still quivering on the ground.

quote.citation: 1851 November 14, Herman Melville, chapter 84, in Moby-Dick; or, The Whale, 1st American edition, New York, N.Y.: Harper & Brothers; London: Richard Bentley, →OCLC, page 410:
quote.text: Next moment with a rapid, nameless impulse, in a superb lofty arch the bright steel spans the foaming distance, and quivers in the life spot of the whale.

quote.citation: 1919 October, John Galsworthy, chapter VIII, in Saint’s Progress, London: William Heinemann, published December 1919, →OCLC, part III, page 300:
quote.text: And the moonlight on the Church seemed to shift and quiver—some pigeons perhaps had been disturbed up there.
